intelligence.human_view: Think of a house with three rooms you actually live in — your own room, your work room, and the room for the thing you love — each with its own jewel on the door, and your letters kept inside the room they belong to. It is also a shop you walk through instead of a brochure you read: by the time you reach the till you have already tried the thing, and the shop's promise is built into the building — there is no back room where someone reads your letters. The family that runs it is twelve siblings on one farm, each master of one part, all drinking from the same well, telling the whole farm's state at one table every day. Every tenant gets the same solid house, finished once, with their own name on the door — never a slightly different shack each time. The postman carries your letters faithfully and never steams one open. And the parent's standard governs it all: you do not say you fed the baby because the bottle was warmed — the baby ate, or she didn't.
intelligence.simple_view: Imagine one house with three rooms: yours, your work, and the place for your favourite thing! Your letters live in the room they belong to, and each room has its own shiny gem on the door. Nobody reads your diary, because your diary stays in your own special box that only you can open. When we show our work, we show the real finished thing, not a drawing of it. And if someone gives you ten jobs, you finish all ten before you show them even one. Being the very best means being wise and kind, not just being fast.
intelligence.grandma_view: It's like this, love — a well-run home has rooms with purposes, dear, and you don't eat in the hallway or keep your letters in a box by the door. A good shopkeeper lets the goods speak, love — you walk in, you see the real thing, you touch it, and by the counter you already know. And a trustworthy shopkeeper never reads the letters you leave in your box with her, dear — she keeps the box locked and hands it back untouched. Trust is a lifetime's work and a minute's loss, love, and love shows in the checking: you taste the soup before it leaves the kitchen, and you make sure the mended coat still has all its buttons.
